Chemo- and Regiodivergent Allyl-Propargyl Cross-Coupling
Reactions for the Construction of 1,4-Enallenes and 1,5-Enynes
Huijun Qian+, Gabriel N. Morais+, Katherine E. Colbaugh, Junqi Su, Zili Chen, Zhiping Li,*
Shuming Chen,* and Leiyang Lv*
Abstract: Catalyst-controlled divergent transformations represent a vital strategy for the efﬁcient production of structurally
diverse molecules from the same readily available precursors. Herein, we report the palladium/phosphine-catalyst-driven
chemo- and regiodivergent allyl-propargyl cross-coupling of propargyl carbonates with allyl boronates. Density functional
theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the bidentate phosphine ligand plays a crucial role in determining the relative
favorability of possible reductive elimination modes from the ƞ3-allyl-ƞ1-allenyl palladium intermediate species. Speciﬁcally,
MeO-BIPHEP facilitates the 1,1 ′-reductive elimination to form the 1,4-enallenes; in contrast, XantPhos favors the
formation of 1,5-enynes through a 3,3 ′-reductive elimination pathway.
Introduction
Chemo- and regiodivergent synthesis has emerged as a
powerful and efﬁcient strategy for the selective synthesis
of different structurally valuable molecules from the same
precursors.[1–4] In this context, the precise manipulation
of reaction intermediates to regulate product distributions
has become a promising approach for designing structural
diversity and complexity.[5–8] This approach depends primarily
on the elaborate selection of appropriate catalytic systems, the
ﬁne-tuning of tailor-made the catalyst structure and/or appro-
priate reagents, which has attracted signiﬁcant attention of
chemists.[9–11] For example, the palladium-catalyzed coupling
reaction of propargyl electrophiles (e.g., propargyl acetates,
esters, carbonates, and halides) with various nucleophiles
has captured the attention of the scientiﬁc community since
Tsuji’s seminal report in 1985. [12] This reaction involves
key allenyl or propargyl palladium species that can facil-
itate allenylation, [13] alkenylation,[14,15] propargylation,[16–21]
dienylation,[22–25] and other related processes. [26–29] Ak e y
concern in these processes is the control of chemo- and
regioselectivity due to the presence of both the propargylic
and allenic palladium species. [30–34] T ypically, allene products

are obtained via the corresponding allenyl palladium species
that generated via S N2’-type oxidative addition or S N2-type
oxidative addition followed by isomerization via a propargyl
intermediate. In a few cases, direct propargyl substitution with
carbon nucleophiles has been achieved as the main product
via the propargyl palladium intermediate (Scheme 1a).
Both propargyl compounds [35–37] and allenes[38–41] are rec-
ognized as valuable synthetic building blocks for a variety of
downstream transformations in organic chemistry. However,
the issue of chemo- and regioselectivity poses a challenge
in cross-coupling reactions involving propargyl/1,2-allenyl
metal species.[42] T o address this problem, Ma and coworkers
realized the regiodivergent Pd-catalyzed Negishi coupling
reaction of propargyl mesylates with (alkoxycarbonyl)ethenyl
zinc reagents, in which the neutral or anionic phosphine ligand
was used to achieve the 1,4-enynes or 1,3-enallenes, respec-
tively (Scheme 1b).[43] Recently, our lab has investigated
palladium/N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed regiodi-
vergent (aza)allyl-ﬂuoroallyl type cross-coupling reactions
of gem-diﬂuorocyclopropanes with ambident nucleophiles
(X = Y-Z−).[44–46] In these transformations, 3,3 ′-reductive
elimination[47] via a seven-membered ring transition state has
been identiﬁed as the key step to enable both the chemo-
and regioselectivity. This reaction mode modality contrasts
with the more common direct 1,1 ′-reductive elimination via
a three-membered ring transition state.
Based on our studies and inspired by the contribu-
tions of Echavarren, [48] Morken,[49–51] and Hou [52,53] on the
palladium/phosphine-catalyzed regiodivergent coupling of
allylic electrophiles with allyl metal reagents, we hypothesized
that the chemo- and regioselectivity in analogous allyl-
propargyl cross-coupling reactions could be modulated by the
selection of appropriate ligands. [54–59] However, in contrast
to allyl precursors, transformations invloving propargylic
derivatives presented several challenges: 1) the coexistence
of both propargylic and allenic palladium species; 2) the
chemo- and regioselectivity issues arising from the interaction

of nucleophilic allylic species with the propargylic or allenic
palladium species; and 3) the predominance of either 3,3 ′-
reductive elimination or 1,1 ′-reductive elimination in the
allyl-propargylic cross-couplings. We hypothesized that tuning
the electronic and steric properties of palladium through
ligand coordination could inﬂuence the relative energy and
reactivity of the propargylic and allenic palladium species,
thus addressing these issues (Scheme 1c).
Here, we present our efforts to develop a palla-
dium/phosphine catalyst-driven chemo- and regiodivergent
allyl-propargyl cross-coupling of propargyl carbonates with
allyl boronates, which enables the highly selective synthesis of
1,4-enallenes and 1,5-alkynes (Scheme 1d). DFT calculations
reveal that the ligands signiﬁcantly inﬂuence the selectivity by
modulating the reductive elimination pathway from the ƞ3-
allyl-ƞ1-allenyl palladium species. Speciﬁcally, MeO-BIPHEP
promotes 1,1′-reductive elimination to form the 1,4-enallenes,
whereas XantPhos favors the formation of 1,5-enynes via the
3,3′-reductive elimination pathway.
ResultsandDiscussion
ReactionOptimization
The investigation commenced with the treatment of propar-
gylic carbonate 1a and allyl boronate 2a in the presence of
palladium acetate (5 mol%), phosphine ligand and base in
THF (T able 1). The 1,4-enallene product 3a was obtained in
77% yield, along with 12% yield of the byproduct 4a when
BINAP ( L1) was used as the ligand. Further investigation
of various bidentate phosphine ligands, including T ol-BINAP
(L2), SDP ( L3), MeO-BIPHEP ( L4), GARPHOS ( L5),
SEGPHOS ( L6), DTBM-SEGPHOS ( L7), revealed that L4
was the most effective ligand for the formation of the allene
product, affording 3a in 92% yield with only 4% yield for
4a. Notably, the yield of the byproduct 4a was increased
to 31% when DPEphos ( L8) was used. This serendipitous
observation prompted us to explore strategies to enhance the
formation of the 1,5-enyne as the main product through ligand
optimization. Encouragingly, the application of Xantphos
(L9) resulted in a signiﬁcant increase in yield of 4a to 90%. We
then evaluated a series of Xantphos-type ligands,[60–62] includ-
ing SiXantphos ( L10), NiXantphos ( L11), N-Bn-NiXantphos
(L12), SulfoXantphos (L13), tBu-XantPhos (L14), XantPhos-
Pd-G2 (L15), XantPhos-Pd-G3 (L16), and another Xantphos-
based ligand ( L17). With the exception of L17, which did not
facilitate the reaction, all other XantPhos-type ligands effec-
tively generated 4a as the major product. Among them, L9
was still the best ligand in terms of both yield and selectivity.
For additional parameters that affect the transformation, see
Ta b l e sS1–S10 for further details.
SubstrateScopefor1,4-Enallenes
The substrate scope of propargylic carbonates for the synthe-
sis of allenes was investigated using MeO-BIPHEP (L4)a st h e
ligand (T able 2). Generally, propargylic carbonates bearing
both electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups
reacted efﬁciently with allyl boronate 2a, delivering the
1,4-enallene products in good to excellent yields. Notably, the
electron-donating substrates exhibited higher regioselectivity
(>16:1). A variety of substituents, including methyl, ethyl,
tert-butyl, phenyl, methoxyl, ethoxyl, phenoxy, ﬂuoride,
bromide, chloride, and triﬂuoromethyl, were well-tolerated
regardless of the para-, meta-, or ortho-substitutions, resulting
in the formation of the corresponding products 3b–3o in 61%–
96% yields under the optimized conditions. Additionally,
propargylic carbonates derived from naphthalene, thiophene
and pyridine were also suitable candidates in this transfor-
mation (3p-3s). Moreover, alkyl propargylic carbonates, such
as methyl non-2-yn-1-yl carbonate and 5-(benzyloxy)pent-2-
yn-1-yl methyl carbonate delivered the desired products
3t and 3u in 78% and 93% yields, respectively, with

bearing the monophenyl substituent was also applicable
and provided the product 4u in 77% yield with excellent
selectivity (>50:1). However, propargylic carbonate with gem-
methyl substitution failed in this transformation. Notably,

Organoboronates
We evaluated the effect of common leaving groups, such as -
OAc, -Boc, and -Cl, on propargylic electrophiles ( 1ai − 1ak).
As summarized in T able 4, the corresponding products ( 3a
and 4a) were obtained under Condition A or Condition
B. However, both the yields and selectivities were inferior
to those achieved with propargyl carbonate 1a (entries 1–
3). Notably, potassium allyl triﬂuoroboronate 2b reacted
efﬁciently with propargyl carbonate 1a to afford the enallene
products 3a and 4a in good yields and selectivities (entry
4). We have also investigated the effect of substituents on
allylboronates for this reaction. When 2-substituted allyl-
boronates, such as 2-methyl allyl boronate ( 2c) and 2-phenyl
allyl boronate ( 2d) were applied, the desired products 5a and
5b were obtained in 75% and 67% yields, respectively (entries
5 and 6).In the case of 3-methyl- and 1-methyl-substituted
allylboronates (2e and 2f), the same product 5c was obtained
in yields of 48% and 35%, respectively (entries 7 and 8). These
results suggest that an S E2’ transmetalation pathway is oper-
ative, with the σ−π−σ isomerization of the allyl-palladium
species prior to the 1,1 ′-reductive elimination. [49–51] Further-
more, when the 1,1-dimethyl-substituted allylboronate 2h was
tested under condition A, the desired product 5e was obtained
in 65% yield (entry 9). However, the 3,3-dimethyl substituted
allylboronate 2h did not give the enallenes 5e or 5f (entry
10), probably due to the high activation energy required
for transmetalation. Notably, the enyne products 6a-6f were
absent under condition B, which was attributed to the high
energy barrier associated with the 3,3 ′-reductive elimination
pathway.[51]

ReactionsofBis-PropargylCarbonatewithAllylBoronate
Encouraged by the above results, we extended this chemo-
and regioselective methodology to the manipulation of
bis-propargyl carbonate 7. We were pleased to observe that
the desired products, bis-allylated allene 8 and enyne 9,w e r e
obtained in 65% and 73% yields, respectively (Scheme 2).
DFTCalculations
T o provide further insight into the reaction, we performed
density functional theory (DFT) calculations. A plausible
reaction mechanism is illustrated in Scheme 3. The pro-
cess begins with an S N2’-type anti-oxidative addition of
propargylic carbonate to Pd(0), resulting in the formation
of the ƞ1-allenyl Pd species C, which can equilibrate to the
propargyl Pd species A through 1,3-Pd shift ( B).[30] From
either the propargyl or the allenyl Pd species, transmetalation
of the allyl boronate then primes the system to undergo the
C─C forming reductive elimination step, which can occur in
either 1,1 ′- or 3,3 ′- fashion to yield the enallene or enyne
product. T o probe whether any of the four possible reductive
limitation modes are inherently more favorable than others,
we ﬁrst performed calculations on small model phosphine
ligand systems including PH 3 and H 2PCH2CH2PH2; both

T o further probe the factors underpinning the relative
favorability of some reductive elimination TSs over others,
we generated non-covalent interaction (NCI) plots for all
reductive elimination TSs (Figure 1). The NCI plot of TS-
2b revealed extensive stabilizing π –π stacking interactions
between the substrate’s phenyl substituent and the tricyclic
core of the XantPhos ligand. Similar, albeit less extensive, π –
π stacking interactions were also observed in the NCI plots of
TS-1b and TS-1c. T o elucidate the role of dispersion interac-
tions (including attractive π –π stacking) in determining the
order of relative free energies of the reductive elimination
transition states, we compared TS energies calculated with
B3L YP (without dispersion) and B3L YP-D3 (with empirical
dispersion). This kind of comparison has been used to
gauge the contribution of dispersion toward calculated energy
differences.[63,64] As T able5 shows, the B3L YP-D3 values rank
the four TSs in the same order as M06-D3, while the B3L YP
values show signiﬁcant qualitative disagreement, ranking TS-
2d as the lowest-energy TS and TS-2b as much higher in
energy. These values underline the important role played
by dispersion effects, including π –π stacking interactions,
in stabilizing TS-2b. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA)
performed on TS-2a–d also showed that TS-2b has the
most favorable interaction energy between the Pd-XantPhos
framework and the substrate fragments, including particularly
favorable electrostatic interaction and charge transfer terms
(see T ableS15 for details).
Another potential contributing factor to the different
ordering of TS free energies between the MeO-BIPHEP
and XantPhos systems is the steric contours of the ligands.
While XantPhos possesses a relatively ﬂat fused tricyclic
core that can accommodate coordinated substrate fragments
in a variety of different orientations, MeO-BIPHEP has a

While these computational investigations results have
revealed important differences in non-covalent interaction
strength and ligand steric proﬁles, we carefully note that
the regioselectivity of this transformation is also signiﬁcantly
impacted by factors such as the identity of the leaving group,
some of which (including acetate or chloride anions) were
found to lower the regioselectivity in increased concentrations
(see T ables S13 and S14 for details). Although the relative
free energies of the reductive elimination TSs provide one
plausible explanation for the divergent regioselectivity in
the MeO-BIPHEP and XantPhos systems, further modeling
efforts will be necessary to address the roles played by leaving
group anions in inﬂuencing the regioselectivity and provide a

Conclusion
In conclusion, we have developed a ligand-dependent chemo-
and regioselective allylation of propargylic carbonates with
allylboronates that allows for the highly selective synthesis of
1,4-enallenes and 1,5-alkynes. DFT calculations showed that
the bidentate phosphine ligands play a critical role in deter-
mining the relative favorability of different reductive elimi-
nation modes from the putative ƞ3-allyl-ƞ1-allenyl palladium
species. Speciﬁcally, MeO-BIPHEP promotes 1,1 ′-reductive
elimination to form the 1,4-enallenes, whereas XantPhos
favors the formation of 1,5-enynes via the 3,3 ′-reductive
elimination pathway. This study provides in-depth insights
into the underlying mechanisms of allylation reactions involv-
ing allenyl-palladium complexes and offers a highly efﬁcient
strategy for chemo- and regiodivergent transformations using
readily available identical starting materials.

Chemo- and Regiodivergent Allyl-Propargyl Cross-Coupling
Reactions for the Construction of 1,4-Enallenes and 1,5-Enynes

Huijun Qian+, Gabriel N. Morais+, Katherine E. Colbaugh, Junqi Su, Zili Chen, Zhiping Li,*
Shuming Chen,* and Leiyang Lv*

Abstract: Catalyst-controlled divergent transformations represent a vital strategy for the efficient production of structurally
diverse molecules from the same readily available precursors. Herein, we report the palladium/phosphine-catalyst-driven
chemo- and regiodivergent allyl-propargyl cross-coupling of propargyl carbonates with allyl boronates. Density functional
theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the bidentate phosphine ligand plays a crucial role in determining the relative
favorability of possible reductive elimination modes from the <sup>3</sup>-allyl- <sup>1</sup>-allenyl palladium intermediate species. Specifically,
MeO-BIPHEP facilitates the 1,1--reductive elimination to form the 1,4-enallenes; in contrast, XantPhos favors the
formation of 1,5-enynes through a 3,3--reductive elimination pathway.
Introduction

Chemo- and regiodivergent synthesis has emerged as a
powerful and efficient strategy for the selective synthesis
of different structurally valuable molecules from the same
precursors.<sup>[1–4]</sup> In this context, the precise manipulation
of reaction intermediates to regulate product distributions
has become a promising approach for designing structural
diversity and complexity.<sup>[5–8]</sup> This approach depends primarily
on the elaborate selection of appropriate catalytic systems, the
fine-tuning of tailor-made the catalyst structure and/or appro-
priate reagents, which has attracted significant attention of
chemists.<sup>[9–11]</sup> For example, the palladium-catalyzed coupling
reaction of propargyl electrophiles (e.g., propargyl acetates,
esters, carbonates, and halides) with various nucleophiles
has captured the attention of the scientific community since
Tsuji’s seminal report in 1985.<sup>[12]</sup> This reaction involves
key allenyl or propargyl palladium species that can facil-
itate allenylation,<sup>[13]</sup> alkenylation,<sup>[14,15]</sup> propargylation,<sup>[16–21]</sup>
dienylation,<sup>[22–25]</sup> and other related processes.<sup>[26–29]</sup> A key
concern in these processes is the control of chemo- and
regioselectivity due to the presence of both the propargylic
and allenic palladium species.<sup>[30–34]</sup> Typically, allene products

are obtained via the corresponding allenyl palladium species
that generated via S 2’-type oxidative addition or S 2-type
oxidative addition followed by isomerization via a propargyl
intermediate. In a few cases, direct propargyl substitution with
carbon nucleophiles has been achieved as the main product
via the propargyl palladium intermediate (Scheme 1a).

Both propargyl compounds <sup>[35–37]</sup> and allenes<sup>[38–41]</sup> are rec-
ognized as valuable synthetic building blocks for a variety of
downstream transformations in organic chemistry. However,
the issue of chemo- and regioselectivity poses a challenge
in cross-coupling reactions involving propargyl/1,2-allenyl
metal species.<sup>[42]</sup> To address this problem, Ma and coworkers
realized the regiodivergent Pd-catalyzed Negishi coupling
reaction of propargyl mesylates with (alkoxycarbonyl)ethenyl
zinc reagents, in which the neutral or anionic phosphine ligand
was used to achieve the 1,4-enynes or 1,3-enallenes, respec-
tively (Scheme 1b).<sup>[43]</sup> Recently, our lab has investigated
palladium/N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed regiodi-
vergent (aza)allyl-fluoroallyl type cross-coupling reactions
of gem-difluorocyclopropanes with ambident nucleophiles
(X Y-Z−).<sup>[44–46]</sup> In these transformations, 3,3--reductive
elimination<sup>[47]</sup> via a seven-membered ring transition state has
been identified as the key step to enable both the chemo-
and regioselectivity. This reaction mode modality contrasts
with the more common direct 1,1--reductive elimination via
a three-membered ring transition state.

Based on our studies and inspired by the contribu-
tions of Echavarren,<sup>[48]</sup> Morken,<sup>[49–51]</sup> and Hou<sup>[52,53]</sup> on the
palladium/phosphine-catalyzed regiodivergent coupling of
allylic electrophiles with allyl metal reagents, we hypothesized
that the chemo- and regioselectivity in analogous allyl-
propargyl cross-coupling reactions could be modulated by the
selection of appropriate ligands.<sup>[54–59]</sup> However, in contrast
to allyl precursors, transformations invloving propargylic
derivatives presented several challenges: 1) the coexistence
of both propargylic and allenic palladium species; 2) the
chemo- and regioselectivity issues arising from the interaction

Results and Discussion
Reaction Optimization

The investigation commenced with the treatment of propar-
gylic carbonate 1a and allyl boronate 2a in the presence of
palladium acetate (5 mol%), phosphine ligand and base in
THF (Table 1). The 1,4-enallene product 3a was obtained in
77% yield, along with 12% yield of the byproduct 4a when
BINAP (L1) was used as the ligand. Further investigation
of various bidentate phosphine ligands, including Tol-BINAP
(L2), SDP (L3), MeO-BIPHEP (L4), GARPHOS (L5),
SEGPHOS (L6), DTBM-SEGPHOS (L7), revealed that L4
was the most effective ligand for the formation of the allene
product, affording 3a in 92% yield with only 4% yield for
4a. Notably, the yield of the byproduct 4a was increased
to 31% when DPEphos (L8) was used. This serendipitous
observation prompted us to explore strategies to enhance the
formation of the 1,5-enyne as the main product through ligand
optimization. Encouragingly, the application of Xantphos
(L9) resulted in a significant increase in yield of 4a to 90%. We
then evaluated a series of Xantphos-type ligands,<sup>[60–62]</sup> includ-
ing SiXantphos (L10), NiXantphos (L11), N-Bn-NiXantphos
(L12), SulfoXantphos (L13), <sup>t</sup>Bu-XantPhos (L14), XantPhos-
Pd-G2 (L15), XantPhos-Pd-G3 (L16), and another Xantphos-
based ligand (L17). With the exception of L17, which did not
facilitate the reaction, all other XantPhos-type ligands effec-
tively generated 4a as the major product. Among them, L9
was still the best ligand in terms of both yield and selectivity.

To further probe the factors underpinning the relative
favorability of some reductive elimination TSs over others,
we generated non-covalent interaction (NCI) plots for all
reductive elimination TSs (Figure 1). The NCI plot of TS-
2b revealed extensive stabilizing π–π stacking interactions
between the substrate’s phenyl substituent and the tricyclic
core of the XantPhos ligand. Similar, albeit less extensive, π–
π stacking interactions were also observed in the NCI plots of
TS-1b and TS-1c. To elucidate the role of dispersion interac-
tions (including attractive π–π stacking) in determining the
order of relative free energies of the reductive elimination
transition states, we compared TS energies calculated with
B3LYP (without dispersion) and B3LYP-D3 (with empirical
dispersion). This kind of comparison has been used to
gauge the contribution of dispersion toward calculated energy
differences.<sup>[63,64]</sup> As Table 5 shows, the B3LYP-D3 values rank
the four TSs in the same order as M06-D3, while the B3LYP
values show significant qualitative disagreement, ranking TS-
2d as the lowest-energy TS and TS-2b as much higher in
energy. These values underline the important role played
by dispersion effects, including π–π stacking interactions,
in stabilizing TS-2b. Energy decomposition analysis (EDA)
performed on TS-2a–d also showed that TS-2b has the
most favorable interaction energy between the Pd-XantPhos
framework and the substrate fragments, including particularly
favorable electrostatic interaction and charge transfer terms
(see Table S15 for details).

Another potential contributing factor to the different
ordering of TS free energies between the MeO-BIPHEP
and XantPhos systems is the steric contours of the ligands.
While XantPhos possesses a relatively flat fused tricyclic
core that can accommodate coordinated substrate fragments
in a variety of different orientations, MeO-BIPHEP has a

protruding toward both flanks of the central P─Pd─P axis
(Figure 2). Calculated steric maps also showed that the
MeO-BIPHEP system experiences more steric pressure at
the potential substrate coordination sites than the XantPhos
system (see Figure S3 for details). In particular, this difference
may partially explain the favorability of the enyne-producing
3,3-reductive elimination mode in the XantPhos system (TS-
2b), in which the phenyl substituent of the substrate must be
placed close to the ligand framework.

While these computational investigations results have
revealed important differences in non-covalent interaction
strength and ligand steric profiles, we carefully note that
the regioselectivity of this transformation is also significantly
impacted by factors such as the identity of the leaving group,
some of which (including acetate or chloride anions) were
found to lower the regioselectivity in increased concentrations
(see Tables S13 and S14 for details). Although the relative
free energies of the reductive elimination TSs provide one
plausible explanation for the divergent regioselectivity in
the MeO-BIPHEP and XantPhos systems, further modeling
efforts will be necessary to address the roles played by leaving
group anions in influencing the regioselectivity and provide a
complete mechanistic picture.
Conclusion

In conclusion, we have developed a ligand-dependent chemo-
and regioselective allylation of propargylic carbonates with
allylboronates that allows for the highly selective synthesis of
1,4-enallenes and 1,5-alkynes. DFT calculations showed that
the bidentate phosphine ligands play a critical role in deter-
mining the relative favorability of different reductive elimi-
nation modes from the putative ƞ<sup>3</sup>-allyl-ƞ<sup>1</sup>-allenyl palladium
species. Specifically, MeO-BIPHEP promotes 1,1--reductive
elimination to form the 1,4-enallenes, whereas XantPhos
favors the formation of 1,5-enynes via the 3,3--reductive
elimination pathway. This study provides in-depth insights
into the underlying mechanisms of allylation reactions involv-
ing allenyl-palladium complexes and offers a highly efficient
strategy for chemo- and regiodivergent transformations using
readily available identical starting materials.
